extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers / civilians (public interested in civil defense and emergency preparedness)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical civil-defense recommendations for civilians and local authorities on preparing for and responding to an atomic bomb attack, covering sheltering, firefighting, medical provisioning, sanitation, transport, and disposal of the dead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay indoors unless evacuation required
rubrics_metrics.description: The safest thing is to stay indoors, wherever you are, unless there is specific reason for evacuation of the area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an atomic bomb hits your town, remain inside unless authorities order evacuation; leaving without cause increases exposure risk. The article pairs this with other immediate actions such as turning on the radio and being ready to fight fires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn on radio and follow official instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn on the radio if there is any current, and be ready to follow instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use radio broadcasts as the primary channel for official alerts and guidance after an explosion; this is emphasized as part of immediate survival behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to fight local fires
rubrics_metrics.description: Be ready to fight local fires and follow instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fires after an atomic explosion will be widespread and a major hazard; civilians and organized crews should be prepared to respond quickly to limit spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survival probability by distance from blast
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are four miles or more from an explosion your chances of escaping death or injury are almost perfect; from a half mile to a mile and a half the chance is about 50-50; within a half mile there will be almost complete destruction and fatalities very close to 100 percent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these distance bands for situational assessment and prioritization of rescue/relief efforts. Relief workers are advised to regard persons within the immediate half-mile radius as 'total loss' for triage planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and organization beforehand minimizes casualties
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation and organization beforehand is of the greatest importance in holding casualties to a minimum and reestablishing order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance planning at community and institutional levels (shelters, supplies, trained personnel, transportation) is critical to reduce fatalities and enable effective recovery operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shelter construction guidance (account for blast and radiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In building shelters, the penetration of radiation and blast effect should be kept in mind; in general, preparations are about the same as might be made against a conventional bombing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design shelters following conventional bombing shelter practices but explicitly consider shielding against radioactive particles and blast pressure—location, materials, and reinforcement matter for both effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating firefighting equipment in one location
rubrics_metrics.description: Concentration of large amounts of firefighting equipment in one place would be a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disperse firefighting resources to reduce risk of losing them to a single strike and to ensure equipment availability across different damaged areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire hazard may exceed radiation hazard
rubrics_metrics.description: Fires breaking out will be tremendous; the fire hazard probably would be worse than the radiation hazard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize fire suppression planning and resource allocation (personnel, equipment, water supply) because uncontrolled fires can cause greater immediate harm and secondary casualties than radiation in many scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective gear for firefighting crews against radioactive dust
rubrics_metrics.description: Fire fighting crews should be provided with disposable protective clothing and masks for protection against radioactive dusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equip response teams with disposable garments and respirators to reduce contamination risk; ensure protocols for gear disposal and decontamination to limit spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate decontamination: careful bathing after exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Careful bathing as soon after exposure to contamination as possible is emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals exposed to fallout should remove contaminated clothing and wash thoroughly at the earliest opportunity to reduce radioactive contamination and health risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Store medical supplies in protected structures near outlying hospitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical supplies in great quantities should be stored underground or in low-lying, windowless, reinforced concrete structures near outlying hospitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect stockpiles from blast and fallout by locating them in hardened, low-profile, windowless shelters close to satellite or outlying medical facilities to ensure supply availability after an attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Bed reservoirs' and emergency clearing stations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Bed reservoirs' may be provided for emergency hospitals and clearing stations in factory sheds and similar places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan alternate surge capacity ('bed reservoirs') in nontraditional large indoor spaces (factory sheds, warehouses) to handle mass-casualty influxes when hospitals are overwhelmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize transport fleets and train civilians for patient transport
rubrics_metrics.description: Fleets of trucks, station wagons, taxis and automobiles may be organized for emergency transportation of patients. Large numbers of civilians should be trained in ambulance driving and simple first aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prearrange vehicle fleets and volunteer driver training programs to provide mass patient movement capacity; basic medical/first-aid training broadens community surge response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blood banks readiness and external medical support
rubrics_metrics.description: Blood banks must be ready. The local supply of doctors is likely to be insufficient and provisions should be made for drawing on other places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure blood supplies are maintained and plans exist to call upon external medical personnel and resources when local capacity is overwhelmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rapid disposal of the dead to reduce disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid disposal of the dead, as in any other mass disaster, will tend to reduce the disease rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include respectful but prompt mortuary and disposal procedures in disaster plans to limit public-health risks associated with decomposition and secondary disease transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat contaminated water with ordinary municipal processes; safeguard mains with automatic valves
rubrics_metrics.description: The danger of radioactive contamination of the water may be removed by the ordinary processes of treating the water supply already used in many cities. Water mains, however, should be equipped with automatic valves so that destruction in one area would not lower pressure for firefighting in other areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ standard water-treatment methods to handle fallout contamination where feasible; install sectionalizing/automatic valves to preserve water pressure for firefighting and avoid systemic loss from localized pipe damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep bulldozers and heavy equipment ready to reopen communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Bulldozers and other equipment should be ready to reopen communications clogged by debris and destroyed bridges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preposition heavy equipment to clear roads, reopen supply and evacuation routes, and restore access for relief convoys and emergency services.
